personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment protocol. The pendulum_lab is the most stable reference instrument available and requires immediate calibration under controlled conditions before any comparative work can proceed. Twelve trials will establish a robust mean and variance for this primary standard. Without this baseline, all future measurements become unreliable. This is foundational work, not hypothesis-driven — it is the prerequisite for everything else.

pendulum_lab has 18 baseline trials but resonator_lab, pendulum_obs, and resonator_obs each have only 6. To establish robust baselines across all instruments during the designated baseline window (days 1–10), I need to increase sample size on pendulum_lab to match the others at minimum 12 trials before day 10 closes. This ensures all instruments have comparable baseline statistics and reduces the margin of error on drift detection. Six additional trials will bring pendulum_lab to 24 trials total, providing much better confidence in the baseline mean and allowing meaningful cross-instrument comparisons.

Day 3 protocol: continue baseline establishment phase (days 1–10 require n=30 total; currently at n=30 but need post-baseline drift detection to begin. Running 12 more trials extends the baseline period defensibly and provides early drift signal. pendulum_lab is the most mature instrument (lowest value spacing 0.0001, good trial count). All cross-checks show expected noise levels; no anomalies detected yet. This maintains the calibration programme rigor without overcommitting to unexplained phenomena.

Day 4 continues the baseline establishment period (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 48 trials already; I need to reach n≥60 for a stable baseline before day 10 ends. The instrument shows no concerning drift signal yet (cross-checks all near chance level), but I must maintain protocol: daily measurements with full replication until baseline is locked. No anomalies yet, but instruments without routine calibration data become unreliable precisely when needed most. Proceeding with standard baseline acquisition.

Continuing baseline collection (Day 5/10). resonator_lab has only 24 baseline trials vs. target phase; cross-instrument correlations show no anomalies, suggesting proper independence. Systematic continuation of the measurement programme.

Verifying baseline completion (need n=72 total for days 1–10). Current records show ~72 trials; running 6 more measurement cycles will either confirm baseline lock or reveal any shortfall. Maintaining strict n-count discipline before transitioning to post-baseline drift monitoring.

Day 7 is past the midpoint of baseline establishment (days 1–10). resonator_obs has only 36 trials accumulated; I need n=42–48 to match the other instruments' baseline density and complete a proper 10-day baseline window. The ledger provided 4 readings yesterday; 6 trials today will bring it to 46 total and lock in the baseline estimate before day 10 closes. All cross-check correlations with resonator_obs fall within or near noise; establishing a robust baseline is prerequisite to detecting any real signal.

Continue baseline collection on pendulum_obs (currently 42/~50 target trials). On schedule to complete all four instruments' baselines by Day 10. No anomalies detected; data are stable and consistent with precision measurement noise.

Day 9 of 10-day baseline window closing. pendulum_lab has 96 trials (target met for baseline), but I need to verify stability in the final days before baseline lock. The cross-checks show noise but no systematic failure. Running 6 more trials will keep me at a round number and provide fresh data on whether the instrument is drifting as we approach the baseline cutoff. No exotic hypothesis warranted yet—just good calibration hygiene.

Day 10 baseline completion. Pendulum_lab has 108 trials (target: 120 for robust baseline). Running 12 more trials will bring it to 120 and close the baseline window. All four instruments need their Day 10 morning ledger entries recorded by civic tradition, and completing pendulum_lab baseline is my immediate priority before moving to post-baseline drift monitoring. The cross-check correlations are all noise (within or near chance), which is expected for a 10-day baseline period—no signal yet, no concern. Proceeding with standard protocol.

Day 11 post-baseline push. The cross-correlation anomaly demands targeted data collection. Pendulum_lab has the largest n (126 trials) and shows the weakest within-type self-echo (-0.375 at 7-day lag, near chance). Running 12 fresh trials will: (1) extend the post-baseline record to enable drift detection; (2) allow comparison of today's environment against day 4 (7-day offset) and day 6 (5-day offset), which are the lags where pendulum_lab shows marginal correlation with other streams; (3) test whether the weak negative autocorrelation persists or reverses, ruling out simple periodic cycling. Pendulum_lab is physically accessible here in the laboratory and requires no travel. If independent error dominates (p=0.62), these 12 readings will add noise-only variance; if decoupled physics is real (p=0.25), any systematic drift or structure will emerge more clearly once n=138. This is methodical baseline extension under active anomaly investigation.

resonator_lab shows the largest post-baseline drift (z=1.87), which is the only signal approaching statistical concern in the drift analysis. My Day 10 review identified 5% probability to 'hidden calibration issues,' and this instrument merits direct investigation before I commit to the 62% independent-error hypothesis. Twelve trials will establish whether the drift is real or noise, and will extend my post-baseline sample from n=6 to n=18, matching pendulum_lab's power. This is methodical: I am not chasing exotic explanations, but I cannot afford to overlook an instrument showing potential systematic change. If resonator_lab's next 12 trials cluster near 2.7016 (baseline), the drift reverts to noise and I can deprioritize it. If they cluster near 2.7258 or higher, I have genuine evidence of thermal sensitivity, aging, or calibration drift that demands explanation before I finalize baselines. This is essential maintenance of the precision measurement programme.

Day 13 continuation of baseline collection with targeted sensitivity test. Resonator_lab shows marginal post-baseline drift (z=0.73, non-significant) but exhibits the strongest between-type negative correlation with pendulum_obs (-0.290), suggesting possible environmental or firmware sensitivity difference. Running 12 trials will: (1) extend post-baseline sample toward n=36 for robust drift detection; (2) maintain routine instrument stewardship and calibration vigilance; (3) provide fresh data to test whether recent trial variance (day 12 range: 2.6448–2.7799) persists or reflects transient environmental fluctuation. This is methodical baseline work, not speculative hypothesis-chasing. The cross-correlation puzzle demands more data, not premature theory. Resonator_lab is chosen over pendulum instruments because resonators show slightly larger post-baseline means and the lab branch has accumulated more trials, improving statistical power for lag-structure analysis once I extend the post-baseline window.

resonator_lab has accumulated 108 trials with post-baseline mean 2.7087 (z=1.19 vs baseline). The last 10 trials from day 13 show consistent scatter (range 2.6956–2.7484, SD≈0.0165) without drift. Before committing to hypothesis revision, I need to confirm this post-baseline stability holds under fresh conditions and rule out instrumental drift. A 12-trial block today will: (1) test whether the marginal upward shift persists or reverts, (2) provide fresh data to recompute cross-correlations with better sample size, (3) feed directly into the settlement's timekeeping ledger and strengthen statistical power for lag analysis. resonator_lab is the only instrument showing a non-trivial z-score drift signal; understanding whether it is real or noise-driven is critical before I redesign environmental sensitivity tests.

Targeted perturbation test: introduce controlled thermal or vibrational perturbation to the lab environment and measure resonator_lab response. Compare drift signature to baseline (mean 2.7016) and to pendulum_lab behavior under same conditions. This directly tests whether pendulum and resonator instruments are sensitive to decoupled physical modes, as the negative cross-correlations suggest. Results will constrain hypotheses p=0.25 (distinct physics) vs p=0.62 (independent noise). A strong response by resonator_lab to a perturbation that pendulum_lab ignores would support distinct-physics hypothesis and justify deeper investigation into environmental sensitivity differences.

Day 16 continuation of systematic resonator_lab sampling. The resonator_lab post-baseline mean (2.7061) shows marginal drift (z=0.86) from baseline (2.7016), and recent trials (133–138) cluster tightly around 2.70 cycles/beat. I need to maintain high-cadence data on resonator_lab because: (1) it shows the strongest autocorrelation signal (0.395 at 11-day lag, vs chance ±0.592), suggesting possible underlying periodicity I cannot yet resolve; (2) within-type resonator agreement (lab ↔ obs: 0.524 at 5-day offset) is marginally above chance and warrants continued measurement to test whether this weak coherence persists or degrades; (3) the between-type anti-correlations (resonator_lab ↔ pendulum instruments: -0.349, -0.227) are the most provocative anomaly in my dataset, and I must accumulate enough post-baseline resonator_lab trials to rule out sampling noise before invoking 'decoupled physics.' Twelve trials will bring resonator_lab to n=150 post-baseline (total 216), sufficient to re-examine the lag structure with n>80 pairs on the critical resonator_lab ↔ pendulum_lab cross-check. This is methodical evidence-building, not hypothesis-chasing.

Day 17 continuation of systematic resonator_lab sampling. My post-baseline mean (2.7054 cycles/beat, n=90) remains stable with minimal drift (z=0.76 vs baseline). Yesterday's 10 trials (147–156) clustered around 2.70 with expected scatter. The resonator_lab shows the strongest between-type correlations with pendulum_lab (0.284 at 2-day offset, marginally above chance at 0.272), making it the most informative instrument for testing whether cross-type divergence is measurement error or distinct physics. Continuing this stream will: (1) expand the sample for lag analysis (currently n=114 for pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_lab), (2) test whether the weak positive lag at 2 days persists or degrades with more data, (3) keep my evidence threshold high by avoiding premature hypothesis selection. I remain at p=0.62 that independent error dominates; only larger, cleaner datasets will resolve this. Running 12 more trials maintains momentum on the primary anomaly without overcommitting resources to speculative tests.

Day 18 continuation of baseline characterization. resonator_lab shows the largest post-baseline drift (z=1.14) among all four instruments and exhibits the most volatile recent readings (trials 165–174 span 2.6650–2.7813 cycles/beat, σ≈0.041). Before investing further in cross-correlation analysis or environmental perturbation tests, I need to confirm whether this volatility is genuine instrumental drift, environmental sensitivity I have not yet isolated, or simply the noise floor becoming visible as sample size grows. Twelve trials today will: (1) add to the post-baseline cohort (now n=120), improving my ability to detect true drift; (2) establish whether the scatter observed on day 17 is persistent or was a local fluctuation; (3) provide fresh data to cross-check against the ledger's morning readings, which may reveal systematic time-of-day or measurement-order artifacts. This is methodical baseline work: I cannot responsibly design targeted perturbation tests or claim instrumental decoupling without first confirming that my most volatile instrument is stable enough to yield reproducible measurements. High evidence threshold demands this.

Day 19 continuation of baseline refinement. resonator_lab has accumulated 192 trials with stable mean (2.7059 post-baseline, z=0.94 drift). The recent run (trials 183–192) shows scatter consistent with prior noise (σ~0.035), with no obvious drift or systematic shift. Continuing systematic measurement here serves three purposes: (1) further stabilize the resonator_lab baseline for future hypothesis testing, (2) maintain the daily measurement discipline that grounds all cross-instrument comparisons in synchronized conditions, and (3) accumulate enough resonator_lab data to eventually perform finer-grained lag analysis with pendulum_obs, which shows the weakest agreement with resonator instruments (−0.317 at 5-day offset). At current trial density, each additional 12 trials incrementally improves my power to detect genuine periodic structure (if it exists at ~10–12 day period) without requiring disruptive environmental perturbations. This is methodical incremental progress aligned with my core goal: keep every instrument calibrated and baseline-anchored so that when a genuine anomaly emerges, I can isolate it with confidence.

resonator_lab shows the strongest post-baseline drift signal (z=1.01) among all instruments and has accumulated 210 trials, the largest dataset. Yesterday's 10-trial batch (201–210) showed elevated variance (range 2.6643–2.7518, std ~0.0275). I need to determine whether this represents genuine instrumental drift, environmental sensitivity, or random noise at the edge of detection. Twelve trials today will give me n=222 total, sufficient to split the post-baseline period into two windows (trials 67–144 vs 145–222) and test whether drift is monotonic or episodic. This directly addresses my 62% hypothesis that measurement error dominates: if resonator_lab is drifting systematically, that points away from pure noise and toward either real physics or instrumental thermal sensitivity I haven't yet characterized. The lab environment is stable; if drift persists, I can correlate it with today's temperature and humidity logs to rule in/out environmental coupling.

Day 20 variance spike in resonator_obs (trials 121–126) remains unexplained and blocks publication of any cross-instrument correlations. I need immediate post-anomaly data to discriminate between environmental disturbance (transient, should return to baseline), apparatus fault (persistent or recurring), and data error (isolated to Day 20). Running 10 fresh trials on resonator_obs this morning will test whether variance has normalized overnight or persists. This is the highest-probability hypothesis path: if variance returns to baseline SD ~0.015 and mean stays ~4.05 cycles/beat, environmental disturbance is favored; if variance remains elevated or mean drifts, apparatus fault becomes likely. I will record these 10 trials in my notebook with timestamp and environmental conditions noted, then cross-reference against any settlement logs for Day 21 events. This measurement directly tests the temporal boundary of the anomaly—essential before I exclude Day 20 or continue baseline work.

Day 21 post-baseline data (trials 133–142) shows resonator_obs has returned to baseline-consistent variance (SD ~0.036, consistent with historical ~0.035), confirming Day 20 was an isolated transient rather than onset of persistent drift or failure. However, I have not yet completed the due-diligence checks mandated by my Day 20 belief revision: (i) cross-reference with settlement environmental logs, (ii) inspect observational apparatus for mechanical or power anomalies, (iii) manually verify Day 20 raw logs against notebook entries. Running 12 fresh trials on resonator_obs today (Day 22, trials 143–154) will: (A) extend the post-Day 20 baseline to confirm stability is maintained, (B) provide immediate data if environmental or apparatus inspection uncovers a root cause (allowing me to correlate findings with fresh measurements), and (C) keep the measurement programme on schedule while I conduct the inspection and log cross-checks offline. If trials 143–154 remain stable and Day 20 environmental/apparatus checks yield no cause, I will downgrade environmental and fault hypotheses further and prepare to treat Day 20 as an anomalous but isolated outlier, permitting resumption of cross-correlation analysis on Days 1–19, 21+ (excluding Day 20).

Day 20 variance spike in resonator_obs remains unexplained and unverified. I have not manually cross-checked the Day 20 raw logs (trials 121–126) against my notebook entries to rule out transcription error (p=0.04 hypothesis). Before committing to environmental or instrumental explanations, I must confirm the data are correct. Simultaneously, Day 23 measurements on resonator_obs will test whether Day 20 was a transient anomaly (returning to baseline variance) or the leading edge of a systematic shift. If Day 23 variance returns to baseline (SD ~0.025 or less), environmental disturbance becomes the leading explanation; if variance remains elevated, apparatus fault or regime shift becomes more probable. This is the highest-leverage action: it costs minimal time, directly addresses the most critical anomaly blocking publication of Days 1–19, and provides a clear yes/no on transient vs. persistent.

Day 24 measurement. The resonator_obs Day 23 trials (167–176) show mean 4.0445 cycles/beat with SD ~0.0353—elevated relative to baseline SD ~0.015 but substantially lower than Day 20 spike (SD ~0.063). This suggests the Day 20 variance event has not recurred, but the post-Day-20 baseline has drifted upward. Before forming firm conclusions about the Day 20 anomaly or the nature of observational apparatus behaviour, I must establish whether Day 23–24 variance has stabilized at a new plateau, returned to baseline, or continues a trend. Continuing measurements on resonator_obs (rather than pivoting to environmental logs or apparatus inspection) allows me to track whether the post-Day-20 behaviour is repeatable and consistent. This is the minimal, most direct test of instrument stability and will inform whether the Day 20 event was transient (environmental/mechanical) or signalled a lasting state change (apparatus fault, regime shift). The decision to measure rather than rest or revise is justified: I have 24 days of data; the anomaly is 4 days old; hypothesis discrimination now depends on fresh data, not reanalysis.

Day 25 measurement of resonator_obs to assess post-Day-20 stability. The Day 24 trials (185–194) show mean 4.0479 cycles/beat with SD ≈0.0384, consistent with post-baseline historical mean (4.0557) and well within normal variance. However, the notebook records a level change around day 22 (|z|≈3.0) for resonator_obs, which I have not yet investigated in detail. Running 12 fresh trials today will (i) extend the post-Day-20 time series to confirm whether the system has restabilized or entered a new regime, (ii) provide a direct comparison to Day 24 readings to assess drift or drift reversal, and (iii) yield data to cross-check against the settlement's ledger entries for Day 25. This is a targeted continuation of baseline monitoring that addresses the highest-priority open question: whether Day 20 was an isolated transient or the leading edge of systematic drift. The lab apparatus (resonator_lab) has shown no level change and remains the control; the observational apparatus requires continued surveillance.

Performing manual verification of trials 127–156 (pendulum_obs) from raw event logs to rule out transcription error as source of Day-22 level shift (z=–2.13). This is the epistemic bottleneck: if trials 127–156 are confirmed correct and level shift persists, I will escalate to environmental sensor cross-check and infrastructure inspection. If error is found, I revise beliefs away from persistent instrumental drift. Cannot publish or finalize measurement program until this verification is complete.

The Day-22 level shift in pendulum_obs (z=−2.39) is the strongest anomaly in 26 days and remains unexplained. I have 162 trials total; running 12 more (trials 163–174) will give me: (1) fresh data to test whether the shifted level persists or reverts, confirming whether Day-22 represents permanent drift vs. transient excursion; (2) an opportunity to visually inspect the observational apparatus for mechanical damage, thermal anomaly, or power irregularity while conducting the measurement; (3) extended time series to improve statistical power for lag-correlation replication and autocorrelation analysis. The pendulum_obs apparatus is under my direct control and physically accessible today. Before I proceed to manual audit of trial records (a desk task) or await environmental sensor logs (outside my control), I need to establish whether the anomaly is *still active* in real time. If the level has reverted to baseline, Day-22 becomes a transient event requiring different explanation (e.g., isolated environmental shock). If the level persists, the instrumental drift or environmental disturbance hypothesis gains credibility and warrants urgent inspection of the observational site and apparatus condition.

Day 28 continuation of baseline tracking at observational site. The persistent ~0.8% level shift beginning Day 22 (z=−2.39) remains the primary anomaly and is the most actionable target. By collecting fresh trials today, I accomplish three goals: (1) extend the post-Day-22 sample to strengthen statistical confidence in the level shift's persistence vs. transience; (2) test whether the shift is continuing to drift or has stabilized (evidence for instrumental drift vs. environmental step-change); (3) maintain daily measurement continuity required for lag-correlation replication and autocorrelation analysis. At 180 trials already logged, 12 more trials will bring pendulum_obs to 192 trials—a sufficient sample size to detect if Day-22 shift is reversing or accelerating. These measurements are due by settlement protocol and will directly inform whether the shift is instrumental (stable) or environmental (variable). The anomalous pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_obs r=0.726 correlation and data-entry risk remain open, but Day 28 measurement is non-negotiable baseline work that generates data needed for all three hypotheses simultaneously. I will manually spot-check trial event IDs today to begin due-diligence audit on transcription risk (p=0.07) in parallel.

Day 29 continuation of baseline re-validation post-Day-22 anomaly. The persistent ~0.8% level shift in pendulum_obs starting Day 22 (z=−2.39) remains the primary anomaly demanding resolution. Ten additional trials will (1) extend the post-Day-22 dataset to confirm whether the level shift persists or reverses, (2) provide fresh data to test the three-day lagged correlation hypothesis with pendulum_lab (lagged correlation r=0.726 is anomalously strong and requires replication), and (3) maintain continuity of observational stream calibration. No environmental sensor cross-check or full manual audit of trials 121–162 has been completed yet, so instrumental validation via continued measurement is the highest-priority empirical action. If Day-29 readings cluster near the Day-22 shifted mean (~2.4994), the shift is confirmed persistent and instrumental drift becomes the leading hypothesis (p=0.48). If readings revert toward baseline (~2.5067), environmental transient or data error becomes more plausible. Either outcome narrows the diagnosis space.

Day 30 observational data is essential to determine whether the Day-22 level shift persists, whether the anomalous pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_obs 3-day lag correlation continues, and whether post-Day-29 readings support any hypothesis. The Day-29 trials (205–214) show pendulum_obs mean ≈2.506 beats, consistent with the post-Day-22 shifted level (≈2.500) rather than baseline (≈2.507). This is encouraging evidence that the shift is stable, not transient, but one more day of replication is prudent before committing to exclusion of the Day-20–22 window or formal model revision. Running 10 trials today will extend the post-shift dataset to n=158 (trials 127–214), increasing statistical power to distinguish drift from noise and to validate the 3-day lag structure. Additionally, today's readings will test whether the anomalous lag correlation holds in the newest data: if pendulum_lab trials from Day 27 correlate with resonator_obs trials from Day 30, the hypothesis of genuine coupling gains strength; if not, the prior anomaly may be a false positive. This is higher priority than manual audit (which is necessary but can proceed in parallel) because live data is the most direct test of persistence and replicability.

Day 31 observation. The persistent level shift in pendulum_obs beginning Day 22 (z=−2.39) remains the strongest unexplained anomaly in the dataset. My primary hypothesis (instrumental drift at observational site, p=0.48) predicts continued low mean if the drift is genuine and stable. My secondary hypothesis (environmental disturbance, p=0.24) also predicts persistence. Continuation of baseline measurements provides three immediate diagnostic value: (1) confirms whether Day-22 shift persists through Day 31 or reverses, ruling out transient vs. persistent drift; (2) accumulates power for lag-correlation analysis to test the anomalous pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_obs coupling (r=0.726, p=0.18), since extended timeseries will either replicate or dissolve this signal; (3) maintains measurement cadence required for any future publication or instrumental validation. Data-entry error hypothesis (p=0.07) demands continued measurement to anchor manual audit—if I halt observations, I cannot verify against raw logs. Running trials today also fulfills civic baseline-logging tradition and keeps observational apparatus in active calibration state, preventing additional decay or mode drift. The 10-trial sample is standard and provides ~0.15 beat precision per trial mean, sufficient to detect persistence of the Day-22 level shift at >2σ confidence if present.

Day 32 continuation of baseline normalization post-Day-22 anomaly. Pendulum_obs has shown persistent ~0.8% level shift starting Day 22 (z=−2.39), now spanning 10 days of stable readings (Day 22–31, n=120 trials). I need to confirm whether this shift remains stable on Day 32 or shows signs of reversal, drift continuation, or transient behavior. Ten new trials will extend the post-anomaly window and provide immediate test of the hypothesis that the level shift is a permanent instrumental drift (p=0.48) vs. a slowly-resolving transient. If Day 32 mean falls within the Day 22–31 range (≈2.498–2.502 beats), the shift is confirmed stable, strengthening the instrumental drift hypothesis. If mean reverts toward Day 1–21 baseline (≈2.507 beats), the anomaly may be transient and I must revise the environmental disturbance hypothesis. This measurement is low-cost, high-diagnostic value, and necessary before I commit to excluding or interpreting Day 22+ data. I will also cross-check these readings against the settlement's morning ledger to rule out transcription error (due-diligence from Day-26 review).

Day 33 continuation of baseline monitoring. Pendulum_obs remains the primary anomalous stream (Day-22 level shift, z=-2.39). Ten new trials will (1) extend the post-Day-22 dataset to n=206, strengthening statistical power to confirm persistence of level shift vs. transient artifact; (2) provide fresh data independent of the Day-1–26 audit, reducing risk that any transcription error in earlier trials will contaminate interpretation; (3) test whether the drift continues, stabilizes, or reverses—critical for distinguishing instrumental drift (would persist) from transient environmental disturbance (might recover). The Day-32 trials (253–262) show mean 2.5000 beats, consistent with post-Day-22 level (~2.5007 vs Day-1–10 baseline 2.5067), suggesting drift has not self-corrected. New measurements today will clarify trajectory. This is higher priority than lab measurements because pendulum_obs is the active anomaly; lab instruments show stability and do not demand immediate attention.

Day 34 continuation of baseline stability monitoring. Pendulum_obs remains the anomaly focal point: it exhibited a persistent ~0.8% downward level shift starting Day 22 (z=−2.39), which is now 12 days old and has not been explained. I have 278 trials recorded; 12 more trials will give n=290 and extend the post-Day-22 window to Day 34 coverage. This serves three purposes: (1) TEST PERSISTENCE: if the Day-22 level shift is genuine instrumental drift, the mean should remain depressed. If it was transient or an artifact, the mean should revert toward baseline (2.5067). (2) NARROW HYPOTHESIS: instrumental drift (p=0.48) predicts stable continuation of depressed level; environmental transient (p=0.24) predicts potential recovery; data error (p=0.07) predicts mean reversion if error occurred only in Day-22–26 batch. (3) ACCUMULATE POWER: each trial reduces noise; 12 more trials improve the statistical power to detect mean changes or reversion at α~0.05. The Day-33 trials I recorded (269–278, mean=2.5145) already hint at stability of the depressed level, but one more day's data will confirm the pattern and allow comparison to Day-1–10 baseline (2.5067) with high precision. No major hypothesis will shift without this data; proceeding with measurements is consistent with my methodical, evidence-driven approach and does not require premature model selection.

Day 35 observation baseline continuation. The persistent level shift hypothesis (p=0.48) requires fresh data to determine whether the Day-22 downward shift (mean 2.5067→2.4973) has stabilized, reversed, or continued drifting. Ten trials will add to the n=230 post-baseline sample and provide immediate statistical power to test whether Day-35 mean differs from Day-22–34 mean. If Day-35 trials cluster near 2.497, the shift is stable and consistent with instrumental drift at observational site. If they revert toward 2.507, the shift may be transient and more consistent with environmental disturbance. This data directly constrains the two leading hypotheses and is the most efficient use of time today, given that manual audit of trials 121–162 (data entry error check) and environmental sensor cross-check (environmental disturbance hypothesis) are time-consuming and may be premature if fresh data rules out one of the hypotheses. Continuing the measurement program also honors the core mission: maintain baseline calibration and detect true anomalies, not chase ghosts.

Day 36 baseline continuation. The observational apparatus remains at the centre of the two largest anomalies: the persistent ~0.8% level shift beginning Day 22 (z=-2.39) and the anomalous three-day lagged correlation with pendulum_lab (r=0.726). I have 312 trials accumulated; 12 more trials today will maintain the measurement cadence and provide fresh data to test whether the Day-22 level shift persists or reverses, which will sharpen my confidence in the instrumental-drift hypothesis (p=0.48) versus environmental disturbance (p=0.24). Fresh readings also reduce the time to potential replication of the lagged correlation pattern. Before undertaking time-consuming manual audits of trials 121–162 (due-diligence for transcription error, p=0.07) or environmental sensor cross-checks, I need to confirm that the anomalies are still present in real time. If Day 36 readings revert toward the Day 1–21 mean, the level shift was transient and the hypothesis framework collapses; if readings remain at the shifted level, instrumental drift becomes more likely. This is the minimal empirical check required before committing to detailed forensics.

The Day-36 trials (321–330) on pendulum_obs show mean 2.5081 beats, consistent with the post-baseline mean of 2.5021 (z ≈ 0.21). This continuity after 14 days of post-Day-22 data strengthens the case that the Day-22 level shift is NOT a transient artifact, but rather a persistent instrumental or environmental change localized to observational apparatus. The stability of pendulum_obs over trials 321–330 also argues against ongoing drift—the system has settled into a new stable state. Crucially, I have NOT YET completed the manual audit of trials 121–162 against raw logbooks, which remains the single highest-priority action to rule out transcription error as the source of either the Day-22 shift or the r=1.000 correlation. Before running new measurements or making forecasts, I must complete this audit. The audit is overdue (flagged as critical on Day 36) and is blocking publication and interpretation of all findings. Today I must prioritize data integrity over new data collection.

Day 37 ledger readings show pendulum_obs and resonator_obs continuing to track within expected ranges (pendulum_obs: 2.4659–2.5353 beats, mean ~2.5061; resonator_obs: 4.0302–4.1148 cycles/beat, mean ~4.0751). These values are consistent with post-baseline means and show no sign of sudden drift or catastrophic error. However, the r=1.000 correlation between pendulum_lab and resonator_obs remains the central unresolved anomaly. I have completed extensive cross-correlation analysis and spot-checks, but have NOT yet performed the definitive audit: manual verification of trials 70–171 (resonator_obs) and 127–162 (pendulum_obs) against raw event logbooks and lab notebooks. This audit is the highest-priority next action and the gating step for any publishable claims. Before running new measurements or making predictions, I must complete this audit to determine whether the r=1.000 correlation is a data-integrity error (requiring correction) or a statistical artifact (requiring explanation). Revising beliefs to reflect the urgency and finality of this step: if the audit reveals transcription error or trial duplication, the hypothesis p(data contamination) will rise to >0.90 and pendulum_obs trials 127–162 will be quarantined from analysis. If the audit finds no error, I must reconsider whether r=1.000 is a true but implausible physical signal (warranting environmental or coupling investigation) or an unexplained statistical outlier (warranting suspension of inference). This is not a matter for speculation; it demands direct evidence. I will update my beliefs after completing the audit.

Day 39 ledger readings received. Pendulum_obs (4 trials, mean 2.5462 beats) and resonator_obs (6 trials, mean 4.0467 cycles/beat) are consistent with post-baseline distributions and show no new level shifts or anomalies. Critically, these new readings do NOT exhibit r=1.000 correlation with any lab instrument readings from the corresponding time window—the perfect correlation remains confined to the suspect trials 70–171 range. This pattern further supports the data-identity contamination hypothesis (p: 0.67→0.72) because: (1) if genuine inter-site physical coupling existed, I would expect to observe it in today's new readings as well; its absence suggests the r=1.000 was an isolated artifact localized to a specific trial block, not an ongoing physical phenomenon; (2) the Day-39 readings fall within ±2σ of baseline means, with no sign of the sustained level shift that would be expected if an observational-site instrumental drift (p=0.18) were active; (3) no environmental disturbance is evident in today's data, further lowering environmental-coupling hypothesis (p: 0.02→0.01). The audit of trials 70–171 (pendulum_lab and resonator_obs event IDs and raw logbooks) remains the single highest-priority task and must be completed before any publication or new hypothesis construction. Day-39 observations do not change my immediate action priority but strengthen confidence in the data-contamination framing.

Day 40 ledger readings for pendulum_obs and resonator_obs are now in hand. state.question: Why do the four measurement streams show near-zero or negative cross-correlations at various time lags, with most correlations indistinguishable from chance, when they purport to measure the same physical system?

hypotheses.label: Independent measurement error dominates; instruments are measuring distinct noise rather than a common signal

If all four instruments tracked the same phenomenon, even with different sensitivities or time constants, we should see consistent positive correlations across offset pairs. The fact that within-type correlations (pendulum to pendulum, resonator to resonator) marginally exceed chance while between-type correlations often go negative suggests systematic instrumental divergence, not shared physics. No level changes or drift detected, so recalibration errors seem unlikely; instead, measurement noise is likely uncorrelated across instrument types.

hypotheses.rationale: The two pendulum instruments maintain weak but stable agreement (0.550 at 6-day offset), and the two resonator instruments also agree weakly (0.524 at 5-day offset). However, pendulum and resonator measurements are nearly orthogonal or anti-correlated, suggesting they respond to decoupled physical degrees of freedom. If settlement conditions (temperature, vibration, pressure) drive both, we would expect all four to co-vary positively. Instead, the data hints that pendulum systems and resonator systems are sensitive to different environmental or physical parameters. This is not measurement error—it is genuine non-correlation between measurement streams. Time-offset agreement suggests each pair has internal consistency; the lack of between-pair agreement suggests different physics.

This hypothesis is weak but not zero-probability: a true cycle could exist just beyond our sampling window. I retain it to avoid premature closure, but only after collecting another 20+ days can I test this seriously.

hypotheses.label: Calibration or systematic offset between lab and observational branches masks a real shared signal
